topic: research metadata; chronology; agent reliability and planning
status: bounded chronology audit from three sampled full texts
claim: Two of three records sampled from the agent_reliability_security × 2010–2014 arXiv-deposit cell are earlier JAIR articles: a 2002 paper first deposited in 2011 and a 2011 paper first deposited in 2014. The third is an IJCAI 2013 paper deposited in 2013. Therefore this sampled cell's arXiv-year composition is not the same as publication-year composition; this observation is not a corpus-wide prevalence estimate.
positive_evidence: The 1106.4570 PDF front matter identifies JAIR 17 (2002), while arXiv lists first submission in June 2011.
The 1401.4606 PDF front matter identifies JAIR 42 (2011), while arXiv lists first submission in January 2014.
The 1304.5159 paper appears in IJCAI 2013 proceedings and was submitted to arXiv in April 2013.
counterevidence: One of the three sampled records has a matching arXiv and publication year.
Only three items from one arXiv-date/topic/selection cell were audited, so the 2/3 ratio cannot be generalized.
falsifiable_test: On a probability sample stratified by arXiv submission year and CS subfield, independently match records to venue/DOI and earliest-public-version metadata; report publication-year offsets and unmatched rates with uncertainty. This cell-level result would weaken as a general warning if offsets are rare across representative strata, and strengthen if substantial systematic lags recur. No prevalence estimate was computed here.
limitations: Three papers from one purposively sampled cell; arXiv deposit year, publication year, and earliest public version can differ. No corpus-wide chronology rate is implied.

topic: multi-agent planning; opponent modeling; autonomous interaction
status: bounded evidence synthesis from one sampled IJCAI full text
claim: I-POMDP Lite proves a policy-loss bound linear in error of predicted opponent strategy, but that theorem does not guarantee that the prediction error is small. The evaluations include an 800-episode intersection scenario against a scripted human-driver model and synthetic POSGs, not human-driver trials. The evidence supports a conditional planning method and a concrete calibration question, not a real-world safety or universal superiority claim.
positive_evidence: Theorem 4 defines opponent-strategy prediction error and bounds policy loss in terms of that error and other task factors.
The intersection scenario includes more than 18,000 modeled states and evaluates 800 episodes with accident and delay costs.
The authors report comparisons across a series of POSGs and describe performance/robustness advantages in those test settings.
counterevidence: The intersection opponent is a scripted model, not a sample of human drivers; no human-subject deployment is reported.
The theorem takes opponent prediction error as an input and does not establish that the proposed predictor is accurate under distribution shift.
The method uses structural assumptions about the other agent's reasoning and sensing; results are tied to the modeled environments and selected baselines.

sources.sections: Theorem 4; Sections 5–6: intersection and POSG experiments

falsifiable_test: Compare I-POMDP Lite, robust/worst-case planning, and simple baselines against held-out human and synthetic opponent populations. Measure opponent-policy calibration error, collision/near-miss rates, delay, reward, compute, and uncertainty across population shifts. The practical claim weakens if prediction error is not calibrated or the advantage disappears under shifted opponents; it strengthens if the theorem's bound and empirical loss track across held-out settings. No human or deployment experiment was conducted in this audit.
limitations: One sampled paper; its guarantees and experiments rely on explicit model assumptions and simulated opponents. No algorithm was reimplemented, and no real-user validation was performed.

topic: temporal planning; plan execution; real-time systems
status: bounded evidence synthesis from one sampled JAIR full text
claim: Drake's random structured benchmarks show large compiled-memory reductions—up to about 700× in the largest cases and commonly 1–10 kB—but also highly variable costs: five large compilations take hours, some cases are up to 100× slower, and a few dispatch outliers reach tens of seconds. The result is a memory/latency trade-off conditional on plan structure, not a blanket real-time suitability guarantee.
positive_evidence: The JAIR evaluation compares Drake with explicit component-STN enumeration on 100 random structured problems per choice size, reaching about 2,000 consistent component STNs.
The reported compiled-representation reduction reaches around 700× on the largest cases; most are around 1–10 kB.
Most small and moderate problems execute in around 10 ms, with most cases under 0.1 seconds.
counterevidence: A few compilation cases take hours; several are up to 100× slower than enumeration, and five largest cases take hours.
A handful of dispatch cases take up to tens of seconds, which the authors say is unacceptable for most applications.
Benchmarks are randomly generated structured plans on a 2.66 GHz machine with 4 GB RAM, not a representative production workload; the authors say application performance may vary.

sources.sections: Section 8.2 and conclusion: benchmark, memory, compile time and dispatch latency

falsifiable_test: Characterize choice count, graph density, overlap, rigid components and other plan features as predictors of tails; benchmark matched workload families on current target hardware and report p50/p95/p99 compile/dispatch latency, peak memory, and deadline misses. The deployment lead weakens if target plans fall in tail regimes or tails cannot be detected beforehand; it strengthens if target workloads exhibit compact representations and bounded latency. No implementation or new benchmark was run here.
limitations: One article's generated structured benchmarks and historical hardware; external validity to current target applications remains untested.

topic: multi-agent systems; game theory; robust decision-making
status: bounded formal-result synthesis from one sampled JAIR full text
claim: Competitive safety analysis establishes payoff guarantees only for specified games and assumptions. Its equality between safety-level and Nash-equilibrium payoff in generic non-reducible 2×2 games requires a strictly mixed safety-level strategy; the paper notes that equality need not hold for a pure strategy. Its 9/8 ratio is proved for a specified extended decentralized load-balancing setting. These results do not establish empirical robustness to deployment model error or failures.
positive_evidence: The article states the strictly-mixed condition for the generic 2×2 equality and distinguishes pure safety-level strategies.
Theorem 2 proves a 9/8-competitive safety strategy for the extended decentralized load-balancing setting.
The paper extends the analysis to specific network and auction models, illustrating that guarantees depend on the formal game family.
counterevidence: The theorem is positive formal evidence within the model; it is not experimental evidence and does not imply the claim fails within its stated assumptions.
Repeated games, mediators, payoff misspecification, and actual network outages are not validated as deployments by these results.

sources.sections: Abstract; Section 5 generic games; Section 7 load balancing; conclusion

falsifiable_test: Perturb payoff parameters and add explicitly modeled communication failures or repeated interaction; separately test whether the formal ratio survives each stated extension and compare safety payoff against equilibrium payoff. The operational lead weakens if small plausible perturbations violate the desired ratio; it strengthens if robustness bounds can be proved for the perturbation class. No new theorem, experiment, or implementation was produced here.
limitations: One theoretical article with model-specific results; the proposed perturbation audit has not been performed and must not be represented as a counterexample to the paper's theorem.
